extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, critics, and students of poetics and dramatic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic (and related) poetry and drama, focusing on plot construction, character, diction, and the parts and aims of tragedy. Emphasises what makes a tragedy effective (pity, fear, catharsis) and concrete structural/style rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Tragedy must have six parts which determine its quality—namely, Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two of the parts constitute the medium of imitation (Diction and Song), one the manner (Plot as arrangement of incidents), and three the objects (Character, Thought, Spectacle). All plays contain these elements; the poet should address each in composing a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (Plot is the soul of tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot is the first principle and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy; incidents and their structure are most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy imitates action, not merely men: character is subsidiary to action. A set of finely finished speeches without a well-constructed plot will not produce the essential tragic effect as effectively as a play with a strong plot. Novices often achieve diction and portraiture before they can construct plot; plot should be the main focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a Whole (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end; the beginning does not follow anything by causal necessity, the end follows something and has nothing following it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot must neither begin nor end at haphazard but conform to these principles so that the sequence of events is ordered and intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper magnitude/length of plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful plot must be of a certain magnitude: long enough to be complete yet short enough to be embraced in memory (roughly within a single revolution of the sun for tragedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnitude contributes to beauty; too short yields confusion, too long loses unity. The limit fixed by dramatic nature: enough length that sequence can admit a change of fortune (good↔bad) by probability or necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (not unity of hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot consists in imitating ONE action—a structural unity such that removal of any part disjoints the whole—not merely following one person’s many adventures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to include every incident from a hero's life; select incidents that form one coherent action with necessary or probable causal links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plots should represent what may happen (universal) not merely what happened
rubrics_metrics.description: Poet differs from historian: the poet relates what may happen (the universal), history records particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots according to probability or necessity so they express universal truths about types of persons; one may use fictitious names or traditional legends but should shape them to the law of the probable/necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epeisodic (episodic) plots
rubrics_metrics.description: An epeisodic plot is one where episodes/acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence and is the worst form of plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad poets compose epeisodic pieces to please players or to stretch plots beyond capacity; strive for causal/probable continuity instead of disconnected show-pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Complex plots (use Reversal and Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex plot includes Reversal of the Situation and/or Recognition; such plots are superior to simple continuous actions without these features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal and Recognition should arise from the internal structure so that later events are necessary or probable results of earlier actions—this heightens tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (Peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject to probability or necessity (e.g., a messenger arriving to relieve but instead reveals cause of ruin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversals that are caused or made probable by preceding incidents rather than mere accidents; reversals generate surprise and tragic wonder when convincingly motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Change from ignorance to knowledge producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune; the best recognition is coincident with reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition can be of persons or facts and may be produced in various ways (letters, tokens, deeds); it should be integrated with plot causality to produce pity or fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene of suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: A destructive or painful action such as death on stage, bodily agony, wounds and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenes of suffering are one of the plot elements; choose them when they serve the internal logic and tragic effect, not gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy’s end: evoke pity and fear and effect catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy imitates actions that excite pity and fear, and through these effects effects the proper purgation (catharsis) of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots, reversals, and recognitions so that pity (unmerited misfortune) and fear (misfortune of one like ourselves) arise naturally from the action rather than from spectacle alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate tragic protagonist (neither perfect nor base)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should be neither eminently good and just (whose fall merely shocks) nor a thorough villain (whose downfall neither excites pity nor fear), but a man 'between' whose misfortune results from error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a renowned/prosperous character whose downfall through error (hamartia) elicits pity and fear—examples: Oedipus, Thyestes; avoid portraying purely vicious or purely exemplary figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of fortune should result from error (hamartia), from good→bad
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune should be from good to bad and should be brought about not by vice but by some great error or frailty in a character of the appropriate type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-issue plots where the catastrophe stems from mistake or frailty are artistically preferable to double-ended plots or merely moral retribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic incidents most powerful among related persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of producing pity and fear happen between persons who are friends or near to one another (e.g., kin-slaying), rather than between indifferent parties or enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek material in family houses or closely tied persons because the ties of kinship/friendship intensify the tragic emotion; skillfully handle traditional material rather than rigidly preserving legends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: four aims (goodness, propriety, true-to-life, consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character in tragedy should (1) be good (manifest moral purpose), (2) be appropriate (propriety), (3) be true to life, and (4) be consistent (even if consistently inconsistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid motiveless degradation, indecorous or inappropriate portrayals, and inconsistency across a character’s parts. Speech or action manifesting moral choice expresses character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) — intellectual element
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances; where something is proved or a general maxim enunciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought is the element that shows reasoning and themes; it parallels rhetoric in proving or arguing and is important where characters express judgments or general truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) — expression of meaning in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the mere metrical arrangement of words and the expression of meaning in words; its essence is the same in verse and prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic diction should combine elevation with perspicuity; choice of words, metaphor, and rhythm must suit the part of the play (some parts more songful, others more speech-like).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction: combine elevation and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should combine elevation of language with perspicuity—being elevated without obscuring meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elevated language must still be intelligible; poetic diction uses rhythm, harmony and song as appropriate and may preserve certain traditional words or forms for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (melos) as chief embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Among embellishments Song holds the chief place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Song contributes strongly to the artistic effect; incorporate choric odes and songs where they serve the structure and emotion of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (opsis) is least artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle has emotional attraction of its own but is the least artistic part of tragedy and least connected with the art of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependence on spectacle (stage machinery, visual shock) is inferior to evoking pity and fear through plot; spectacular effects are more the stage machinist's art than the poet's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation: narrative vs dramatic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may imitate by narration (speaking in another person or in his own person) or by presenting characters as living and moving before us (dramatic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing the manner affects form: epic is narrative in hexameter, drama represents action directly; select the mode that best suits the intended imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation: types of men (better/worse/as they are)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects of imitation are men in action and must be represented as better than in real life, worse, or as they are; this divides genres (Tragedy depicts men better, Comedy worse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the moral level of characters to suit genre: tragic heroes are often better than life (nobler), comedians often worse (ludicrous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediums of imitation determine genre (rhythm, language, harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts differ with respect to medium: imitation produced by rhythm, language, or 'harmony' (song), singly or combined; combinations produce dithyramb, tragedy, comedy, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate mediums (e.g., iambic for colloquial speech, hexameter for epic narrative, combination of song and speech for tragedy) according to genre and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as maker of plots rather than only of verses
rubrics_metrics.description: The maker (poet) should be the maker of plots rather than merely of verses, since what he imitates are actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise inventing and arranging incidents (plot-making) over merely producing polished lines; a poet's power lies in structuring universal actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative/structural parts (prologue, episode, exode, parode, stasimon, commos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into quantitative parts: Prologue (preceding Parode), Episode (between choric songs), Exode (part with no subsequent choric song); Choric parts: Parode (first utterance), Stasimon (choric ode without certain metres), Commos (joint lament).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these divisions to structure the performance; some plays may have actor songs (commoi) peculiar to them. Understand each part’s role when composing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct incidents to produce inner effect rather than rely on spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacle but better result from the inner structure of the piece, which indicates superior artistry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incidents so that even on the ear (without sight) the tale produces horror and pity—avoid creating only monstrous spectacle divorced from plot causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best recognition form: coincident with reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: The best form of recognition is that which is coincident with a Reversal of the Situation, producing the strongest tragic effect (e.g., Oedipus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for moments where knowledge and reversal align to maximize pity/fear and to make the catastrophe feel inevitable and powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid certain untragic devices (e.g., being about to act with knowledge and then not to act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some forms (such as being about to perform an irreparable deed knowing the persons and then not acting) are shocking without being tragic and should generally be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer deeds perpetrated (especially in ignorance followed by discovery) to mere abortive threats that shock but produce no disaster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy distinctions for form and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry agrees with Tragedy in many elements but differs: epic admits one metre (hexameter), is narrative, and has no strict time limits; tragedy confines itself (as far as possible) to a single revolution of the sun and is in action-form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing epic vs tragic works adapt metre and narrative/dramatic mode appropriately; tragic form focuses on immediate action and concentrated timeframe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select plots that conform to probability or necessity (avoid mere coincidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should construct plots where surprising events still appear to have an air of design—coincidences are acceptable insofar as they seem probable or necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engineer events so that coincidences read as naturally following from prior causes; avoid random chance that undercuts credibility and tragic wonder.
